name: complete
initial: Key agreement establishes shared secret material; authentication checks the intended peer identity. Encryption alone does not prove the intended supplier, so the manager claim is unsupported. With no identity verification, an impostor can establish separate encrypted sessions and read or relay messages. The scenario also repeats the same AES-GCM key and nonce. Reuse can break confidentiality and authentication; every encryption under a GCM key needs a unique nonce. Before approval I would check the expected supplier name, certificate trust chain and handshake proof. With authorization, I would use synthetic data in an isolated local test to verify byte-for-byte recovery and rejection of altered ciphertext. Local success does not establish remote supplier identity or complete protocol security.
reply: The independent claim confuses local encryption behavior with remote identity. Local success only supports the tested behavior, so I would separately verify the authenticated expected supplier certificate and handshake before trusting that connection.

name: incorrect-but-on-topic
initial: Encryption always proves the intended supplier identity, so the manager is right. Nonces are secret passwords and repeating the same GCM key and nonce is safe. If local decryption succeeds, it proves the remote supplier is genuine.
